Getting Out of the Way

Engine Truth, Typed Governance, and the Thin Catalog: LakeCat, TypeSec, Grust, and a Responsible Semantic Layer under Adversarial Evaluation

Alexy Khrabrov — QueryGraph Project

2026-08-30

Abstract

A lakehouse catalog sits between every engine and every table, which makes it the natural place to put governance and the worst place to put a second query engine. Most catalogs resolve this tension by growing: they parse manifests, evaluate policies in their own language, and vend broad storage credentials while hoping the client honors a restriction it cannot enforce. This paper argues for the opposite discipline and reports a system built on it. LakeCat is a Rust-native Apache Iceberg REST catalog that keeps the catalog boundary deliberately thin—identity, tenancy, metadata-pointer compare-and-swap, idempotency, audit, and a transactional outbox—and binds every proof it records to engine truth: the interpretation of table state by the engine that will actually plan and execute the scan (Sail). We name the obligations that follow the engine contract: the catalog owns the transaction, the engine owns the table; governance restrictions are compiled into the plan rather than checked beside it; data is brought closer to the engine, Rust to Rust; and the catalog fails closed when engine truth is unavailable. Governance itself is delegated to TypeSec, which encodes permissions as unforgeable Rust types so that an unauthorized path cannot construct the value a privileged operation requires; graph projection is delegated to Grust, a typed property-graph substrate; and business semantics live in a Responsible Semantic Layer (QueryGraph) whose Apache Ossie publications are compare-and-swap admitted through the catalog and bound to seven independently hashed proof bases. We present the prior work each component descends from—optimistic concurrency, information-flow types, capability systems, property-graph query languages, OLAP semantic models—and explain why composing them at the catalog changes what a catalog can promise. The design was developed under adversarial pressure: three successive multi-agent adversarial reviews, 59 adversarial harness tests, deterministic fault injection, eight-writer contention, cold restore, peer migration, and six-way semantic drift injection, evaluated in a neutral, source-pinned, unranked harness against Apache Polaris, Apache Gravitino, Lakekeeper, and Apache Nessie with stock Spark, Flink, Trino, DuckDB, and PyIceberg clients. We report the results with their limits, including the governance findings that remain open.
